item.title: Bill White: A different perspective on artificial intelligence
item.description:
I received wonderful responses to my columns this summer about Fenway Park, artificial intelligence and golf, so I thought I would share a small sampling today.
#### Artificial intelligence We’ll start with the AI column, in which I admitted I’m glad I’ve retired from teaching because of the challenge posed by students using AI to do their writing assignments.
I got a really interesting response from a friend who has worked with educators and students as part of his cybersecurity business. He offered a perspective I hadn’t considered, writing in part:
“When I talk to school administrators about their biggest AI fears in education, they almost all start with student cheating. It’s a legitimate problem. They are very afraid that their kids cheat with AI and won’t learn the material.
“When I ask the students about their biggest AI fears in education, they say something completely different. They are afraid of being accused of cheating with AI. In fact, every student in my class had a horror story about how they innocently submitted a paper or an assignment and some random AI checker flagged it as fake, and they either got a zero or had to explain themselves to their angry teacher. Some of these students are deliberately adding typos and weird syntax into their assignments because the AI sniffers won’t pick it up as easily. The students told stories of arbitrary judgments by different teachers, multiple AI checking tools with inconsistent outcomes, and a lack of written appeals processes.
“Essentially, the constant suspicion by teachers that their students are cheating with AI is destroying the trust that they need to teach them.
“In all the articles I’ve seen written about cheating and AI, I’ve never seen one focusing on this aspect of the problem.”
That was an eye-opener for me. If any educators or students would care to respond, I’d love to hear from you.

**Heinz and colleagues evaluated a generative AI chatbot for adults with clinically significant depression, anxiety, or elevated risk for eating disorders.**
**Users of the chatbot experienced greater symptom reductions compared to controls on the waitlist and reported higher engagement.**
Heinz and colleagues evaluated Therabot, a generative AI chatbot’s effectiveness in treating symptoms of major depressive disorder (MDD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and clinically high-risk feeding and eating disorder (CHR-FED). Compared with controls, Therabot users experienced significantly greater reductions across all three symptom domains at four and eight weeks of usage.

item.title: The next frontier is not artificial intelligence, it’s artificial societies
item.description:
The more interesting possibility is messier – and requires a step-shift in our thinking, from [artificial intelligence](https://theconversation.com/topics/artificial-intelligence-ai-90) to [AI societies](https://blog.lboro.ac.uk/vice-chancellor/2026/08/17/the-age-of-ai-societies/).
AI is no longer just generating an answer – it is doing something about it.
